study.title: Ecclesiastes 5 Reverence before God, limits of words and simplicity before riches
study.overview: Ecclesiastes 5 gathers practical warnings about how the creature must stand before God and before life. The chapter begins with the correct posture in the house of God: to listen with reverence, to speak carefully and to avoid promises made with lightness. Then it denounces verbal arrogance and religious haste, showing that God is not treated as equal human, for he is above and the human being must respond with fear. Then the text expands the reflection for public and economic life: there is oppression, bureaucracy, inequality and attachment to money, but all this remains empty and unstable. Finally, the chapter offers a positive conclusion: the true good is to receive with gratitude the food, drink, work and riches as gifts of God, without the illusion that they can give definitive security.

outline.title: Reversing posture in the house of God
outline.explanation: The text guides to enter carefully, listen more than to speak and avoid hasty words before God. Excess speech is linked to foolishness and lack of spiritual discernment.

outline.title: Votes, words and fear of God
outline.explanation: Promises made to God must be fulfilled without delay, because God is not pleased with empty vows. The conclusion is that reverence, and not verbosity, must govern the relationship with it.

outline.title: Social injustice and the vanity of riches
outline.explanation: The chapter observes oppression, authority over authority, greed, insomnia and suffering caused by accumulated goods. The riches can disappear, hurt the owner himself and do not accompany the person in death.

outline.title: Receiving Life as God's Gift
outline.explanation: In contrast to greed, the text calls to enjoy with gratitude the work, food and drink as part of the divine gift. Whoever receives it with joy lives with less inner weight, because God gives him contentment.

study.context: The chapter reflects on the religious, civil and economic life of the people, with attention to the house of God, to government and daily work. The notes highlight that the place of worship is of everything a place of listening, not to multiply words; and that reflection on vows, oppression and riches serves to correct human vanity. The text also presupposes the reality of administrative authority and agricultural work, without detailing specific historical events.
study.theology: Chapter theology is marked by three axes. First, God is transcendent: he is not domesticated by human words, so worship requires fear, listening, and sincerity. Second, true religion includes concrete fidelity: vote made is a fulfilled vote, because speaking before God has moral weight. Third, good life is not born of accumulation, but of the grace of receiving and enjoying with gratitude what God gives. The chapter corrects both empty religiosity and trust in possessions, and proposes a spirituality of reverence, contentment and responsibility. The prospect is not of contempt of labor or goods, but of moderate and grateful use, recognizing that they are gifts and not gods.

scholarViews.insight: The house of God is of everything of reverent listening; there, words must be measures and promises, careful.
Promises made to God create serious obligation: one should not make a vow lightly, and what has been promised needs to be fulfilled.
The chapter ends by teaching that the believer should thank and enjoy with simplicity the gifts of God, without being dominated by wealth.

questions: Is my presence in worship more marked by listening and reverence or by haste and excessive speech?
Have I treated promises made to God as serious commitments or as momentary words?
How can I receive my work, food and resources as gifts from God, rather than making them my security center?
study.practice: This week, practice a more silent and attentive adoration: pray with few words and sincerity, read the text with delay and examine whether there is any pending spiritual commitment that needs to be honored. Also observe your habits with money and consumption: thank you before using your resources, share with real need and choose contentment instead of anxiety. The chapter calls for a life in which fear of God, integrity and gratitude walk together.
